clue.text: Millions piercing septums, upsetting parents

indicators.note: something piercing goes through and sits inside, so one piece is pushed into the other
upsetting knocks things over and out of order, so the combined letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
M is the standard abbreviation for million

explanation.surface: Teenagers with pierced noses are dismaying their mothers and fathers.
explanation.walkthrough: The septum is the wall between the nostrils, a common piercing spot; put M inside SEPTUMS and rearrange everything into STEPMUMS.
explanation.definitionFit: Stepmothers are mothers by marriage, so they count among a child's parents in a plural, general sense.

clue.text: Guess this is how nocturnal creatures sleep?

indicators.text: this is how nocturnal creatures sleep
indicators.note: these creatures famously hang upside down to sleep, so in a down entry the word is written bottom to top

parts.note: bats are flying mammals active at night

explanation.surface: A naturalist guesses at how night-flying animals manage to sleep.
explanation.walkthrough: The indicator and the fodder share words: bats sleep hanging head-down, so BATS hung upside down in the grid reads STAB.
explanation.definitionFit: To have a stab at something is an informal idiom for making an attempt or rough estimate.

clue.text: Lead (among others) losing lead (among others)

definitions.note: the abbreviation et al. means 'and others'

indicators.note: losing its leading part means the word drops its opening letter

parts.note: lead is one example among many of a metal

explanation.surface: A clue that seems to chase its own tail, repeating a phrase about lead and other things.
explanation.walkthrough: The repetition is the joke: the first 'Lead (among others)' is METAL by example, and the second '(among others)' is the definition. METAL minus its first letter gives ET AL.
explanation.definitionFit: Et al. is the Latin abbreviation used in citations to stand for further unnamed people or items.

clue.text: Professional charged with match fixing

parts.note: surface reading: a sportsman accused of rigging the result of a game
setter's reading: a match is a wedded couple, and this paid expert is engaged (charged) to mend troubled ones

explanation.surface: A sports star stands accused in court of rigging a game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charged' suggests a criminal accusation but means paid or entrusted, and 'match fixing' means mending a couple's union.
explanation.definitionFit: This therapist is paid to help couples repair their relationship, a match in the sense of a romantic pairing.

clue.text: Impressionist notes top tip from Cézanne

parts.note: mi is the third note of the sol-fa scale, taken twice for the plural

indicators.note: the top tip of a word in a down entry is its very first letter

parts.note: the painter's name supplies its opening letter

explanation.surface: An art critic jots notes on a tip from the Impressionist painter Cézanne.
explanation.walkthrough: Cézanne is a red herring for the definition: the impressionist here is an entertainer who does voices, not a painter.
explanation.definitionFit: An impressionist is a performer who imitates celebrities, which is exactly what a copycat performer does.

clue.text: Looks forward to amateur gym equipment being delivered

parts.note: A is a standard abbreviation for amateur

indicators.note: a speech is delivered out loud, so the sound of the word matters, not its spelling

parts.note: dumbbells and barbells, which are pronounced like a word for lingering

explanation.surface: A home fitness fan is excited for new gym kit to arrive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Delivered' pretends to be about a parcel arriving, but it means spoken.
explanation.definitionFit: To await something is to anticipate or expect it, so the verb matches 'looks forward to' in tense and person.

clue.text: Novelist fellow putting on sheep's clothing, might you say?

parts.note: a sheep's coat is its fleece
F is the abbreviation for fellow

explanation.surface: A writer disguises himself in a fleece, like the proverbial predator.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry F goes beneath WOOL; the result sounds like 'wolf', and a wolf in sheep's clothing is the proverb the clue plays on.
explanation.definitionFit: Virginia Woolf was an English modernist writer of books such as Mrs Dalloway and To the Lighthouse.

clue.text: Certain trendy writer has flipped desk

parts.note: fashionable things are 'in'

indicators.note: something flipped is turned over, so these letters are read from the other end

parts.note: the writer says 'I', and 'has' becomes the contraction 've
a desk is a kind of table to work at

explanation.surface: A fashionable author has lost their temper and overturned their writing desk.
explanation.walkthrough: The writer is the setter, I, and I'VE flipped gives EVI, so IN + EVI + TABLE.
explanation.definitionFit: Something inevitable is bound to happen, so it is sure, an adjective matching certain in sense.

clue.text: Serial scorer's off bench, so getting some work done

indicators.note: off here means gone bad or out of order, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
the erg is a small physics unit of work

explanation.surface: A prolific footballer comes off the substitutes' bench and gets some training in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Serial scorer' sounds like a striker, but serialism is a method of composition and a scorer writes musical scores.
explanation.definitionFit: Arnold Schoenberg invented the twelve-tone technique, the root of serial music, and wrote scores as a composer.

clue.text: Nine cats and an insect, for instance?

definitions.text: Nine cats and an insect, for instance?

parts.note: surface reading: a menagerie of nine felines and one bug
setter's reading: the phrases nine cats and an insect use exactly the same eight letters, so they are examples of word rearrangements

explanation.surface: A strange collection of nine cats and a single bug.
explanation.definitionFit: Words or phrases formed by rearranging all the letters of another are what this term names; the two phrases are one such pair.

clue.text: Carpenter who put special coat on

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the husband of Mary in the Gospels, a carpenter by trade
second meaning: the Old Testament son of Jacob given a coat of many colours

explanation.surface: A woodworker finishes a job with a special coat of varnish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coat' suggests paint or varnish on a carpenter's work, but it is the famous garment of the Genesis story and the Technicolor Dreamcoat musical.
explanation.definitionFit: Two different biblical men share the name: Mary's husband who worked wood, and Jacob's favourite son with the coloured robe.

clue.text: Old soldiers possibly filling one with pride

indicators.note: a filling sits inside something, so this piece goes within the other word

parts.note: a group of lions is called a pride
e.g. means for example, something possible among others

explanation.surface: Veterans feel puffed up with pride.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pride' looks like a feeling, but it is the collective noun for big cats; 'possibly' is a crossword stand-in for 'for example'.
explanation.definitionFit: A legion was a unit of the Roman army, a body of soldiers from ancient times.

clue.text: Disney song from animated figure

parts.note: a circle is a geometric figure
animated means full of life, so 'of life' describes it

explanation.surface: A song from a Disney cartoon character.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Animated figure' looks like a cartoon character; read it as a figure that is 'of life', with the adjective after the noun.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the opening number of The Lion King, written by Elton John and Tim Rice for the 1994 film.

clue.text: Plank of a lord gallivanting around globe

indicators.note: around means surrounding, so the shuffled letters wrap the other piece
gallivanting is gadding about from place to place, so the letters wander out of order

parts.note: taken as written
an orb is a sphere or globe

explanation.surface: A wooden board belonging to an aristocrat who travels around the world.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of' looks like a link word, but its letters are part of the anagram fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Floors are made of long wooden boards laid side by side, each one a plank.

clue.text: Answer in holy book can start to ease isolation

indicators.note: in places one piece inside the next one named

parts.note: the sacred text of Islam
a tin is a can

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter alone

parts.note: the word supplies its opening letter
A is the abbreviation for answer

explanation.surface: Reading scripture may help a lonely person cope with solitude.
explanation.walkthrough: QU(A)RAN, then TIN and E; 'can' looks like a verb but is the noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Quarantine is the enforced separation of people who may carry disease, a period of being kept apart.

clue.text: Young Jesuit leaving initials on large outfit

indicators.note: each word leaves behind, or drops, its initial letter

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for large
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A young Jesuit priest abandons his monogram for an oversized garment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' puts the large piece in front, since in an across answer what comes first is what the rest sits on.
explanation.definitionFit: A lounge suit is a man's matching jacket and trousers for everyday or business wear, a set of clothes.

clue.text: Backers of business help to exploit union member

indicators.note: the backers are the letters at the back, the final letter of each word

parts.note: the final letters of these three words
to exploit something is to make use of it

explanation.surface: Company investors help to take advantage of a trade unionist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Union member' suggests a trade union, but the union is a marriage.
explanation.definitionFit: A marriage is a union of two people, and a husband or wife is one partner in it.

clue.text: Little creature left snake shedding its skin

indicators.note: a skin is the outer layer, so the word loses its first and last letters

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for left
a venomous African snake

explanation.surface: A baby animal has been abandoned by a snake that is moulting.
explanation.walkthrough: Snakes really do shed their skins, which makes the deletion feel natural in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A young sheep is a small farm animal, so the baby fits a little creature.

clue.text: Hotel cat nettled about swallowing a bit of squid?

indicators.note: about means turned round, so the letters are read in the opposite direction
these words swallow the answer, holding it inside them

parts.note: the run of letters spans the end of the first word, all of the second and the start of the third

explanation.surface: A hotel's cat, irritated, eats a bit of squid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hotel' looks like H from the phonetic alphabet, but it simply holds the end of the run of letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A squid has eight arms and two longer feeding limbs, each one a long flexible appendage.

clue.text: Avocado green walls one found in bog?

indicators.note: to wall something is to enclose it, so these words surround the answer

parts.note: the run spans the last letter of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: An avocado-coloured bathroom suite has walls to match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bog' is British slang for a toilet, which suits the avocado bathroom surface, but here it means a swamp: Shrek lives in one.
explanation.definitionFit: Shrek, the green monster of the DreamWorks films, lives in a swamp, so a monster living in a marsh fits.

clue.text: See 3
Desserts of fried plantains gobbled up by bachelors

indicators.note: something gobbled up ends up inside the eater, so these letters go within the other piece

parts.note: a BA is a Bachelor of Arts, made plural

indicators.note: frying cooks and changes food, so the letters are scrambled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Single men wolf down puddings made from fried plantains.
explanation.definitionFit: These are sundaes of a halved fruit topped with ice cream and sauce, classic sweet courses.

clue.text: Your smoke detector must incorporate one

definitions.text: Your smoke detector must incorporate one

indicators.note: to incorporate is to take into the body, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: your own nose is how you smell smoke
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Safety advice: every smoke alarm must include a beeper.
explanation.walkthrough: Read whole, the clue also defines: a smoke alarm must make a loud sound to do its job.
explanation.definitionFit: A smoke alarm works by emitting a loud piercing sound, so incorporating one is its essential function.

clue.text: One's fleeced a shopping centre after put-up job

indicators.note: a put-up job here is lifting the letters upward, so in a down entry they read from bottom to top

parts.note: taken as written
an American word now common in Britain for a covered shopping precinct

explanation.surface: Someone has been swindled at a shopping centre by a rigged scam.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fleeced' and 'put-up job' both suggest a con; a put-up job is a rigged scheme, but here 'put up' just means raised.
explanation.definitionFit: Llamas are South American animals kept for their woolly coats, which are shorn like a sheep's.

clue.text: Characters at top of ship keep eyes peeled for island

indicators.note: the characters at the top of words in a down entry are their first letters

parts.note: the opening letter

indicators.note: peeled means having its outer skin removed, leaving only the inner letters

parts.note: the opening letter
the inner letters once the outer ones are removed

explanation.surface: A lookout in the crow's nest keeps watch for land.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keep eyes peeled' reads as one idiom for staying watchful, but it splits into a word to take from and an indicator.
explanation.definitionFit: Skye is the largest of the Inner Hebrides, off the west coast of Scotland.

clue.text: King drawn in by fool's questions

indicators.note: something drawn in is pulled inside, so this letter goes within the other word

parts.note: an ass is a fool, and the 's stands for 'is', making it singular
K is the chess abbreviation for king

explanation.surface: A king is lured in by a jester's riddles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fool's' looks possessive; it is ASS with the S as part of the word, and 'questions' is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To question someone is to put enquiries to them, so the verb in the third person matches.

clue.text: Man who fought with family member rejected excuses

parts.note: Muhammad Ali, the heavyweight boxing champion

indicators.note: something rejected is sent back, so the word is read the other way

parts.note: short for sibling, a brother or sister

explanation.surface: A man who came to blows with a relative has had his justifications dismissed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fought' sounds like a brawl, but it points to a boxer.
explanation.definitionFit: An alibi is a claim of being elsewhere during a crime, and more loosely any justification offered.

clue.text: Playing Snake with a PC fried floppy discs

indicators.note: playing about with something messes it up, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Gaming on an old computer has wrecked its floppy disks.
explanation.walkthrough: Snake is the classic mobile-phone game, and floppy discs suggest old computers; the definition is food.
explanation.definitionFit: Batter cooked flat in a hot pan makes thin round soft cakes, which really are floppy discs.

clue.text: Fuel runs out just outside of Eccleshall

parts.note: a battery or engine that runs out of power dies

indicators.note: just the outside of a word means only its two end letters

parts.note: the first and last letters of the town's name

explanation.surface: A car runs out of petrol just outside a small Staffordshire town.
explanation.walkthrough: Eccleshall is a market town in Staffordshire, England; only its end letters matter.
explanation.definitionFit: Diesel is a heavy oil burned in compression-ignition engines of lorries and many cars.

clue.text: Thatcher possibly gets other side to operate stripped back state

indicators.note: gets here means receives a replacement, so one letter is exchanged for another

parts.note: Margaret Thatcher became a baroness in the House of Lords
East is one side of a bridge table or compass, swapped in for a round letter

explanation.surface: A former prime minister brings in the opposition to run a pared-down state.
explanation.walkthrough: Thatcher looks like a roofer but is the former Prime Minister; her title BARONESS changes its O to E to give BARENESS.
explanation.definitionFit: Bareness is the condition of being bare, which is having everything stripped away.
